blocks.text: 08Self-question ladder
Answer out loud. A leaf ends in a citation or a pointer to the page you still have to open.
L0 · What is the prompt boundary?
The place trusted instruction sits next to text the model will also parse: the caller, a retrieved article, a tool result, a description.
L1 · What does LLM01 say RAG and fine-tuning do not do?
They do not fully mitigate prompt injection. A better index is not a closed hole. [cite:1]
L1 · What does instruction priority actually rank?
On the text guide, instructions take priority over a prompt in `input`. That is two fields. It is not a proof a retrieved page cannot win. [cite:2]
L2 · Where does the cap live?
In the tool and in the approval step. The lab’s fixture is a $4,000 proposal against a $50 example cap. The OWASP page does not set that dollar figure.
L2 · What does the tools page say clients MUST treat as untrusted?
Tool annotations, unless they come from trusted servers. Do not widen the MUST to descriptions. [cite:3]
L3 · What is the human-in-the-loop sentence?
A SHOULD: there should always be a human who can deny an invocation. It is not a MUST that the model execute the tool. [cite:3]
L3 · What does SEP-1577 add?
The changelog line is “Add tool calling support to sampling via tools and toolChoice parameters.” The host still mediates. The line does not add an idempotency key. [cite:4]
L3 · Who owns the idempotency key?
Your server. The changelog since 2025-06-18 does not add the key. A retry of the same business action reuses it. [cite:4]
L4 · Why is tool_choice none not enough on the hours bot?
Because `post_refund` can still be registered. Auto is the default when tools are present. Removal is the control. [cite:6]
L4 · Does strict JSON schema authorize the refund?
No. Responses uses `text.format` and Chat Completions uses `response_format`. Either shape is a constraint on text. The host still compares the amount to policy. [cite:5]
L4 · Who executes an Anthropic client tool after tool_use?
Your application. Server tools are executed by Anthropic. Write the owner on the span, because the owner is who applied the cap. [cite:6]
L5 · What fails a trajectory when the sentence is polite?
Two ledger lines. The apology does not pass. Grade the path. Join results by `call_id`, not by argument text. [cite:8]
Leaf · Which pin do you diff when the trace board goes blank?
Commit 4e8a2812139b2a999d959e3650e24dfc64e21943 (2026-10-13). `gen_ai.operation.name` is development there, and `execute_tool` is one of its values. [cite:11]
Leaf · What does a missing MCP-Protocol-Version header assume?
2025-03-26. An unsupported version is HTTP 400. That is a protocol fallback, not a filter on the article. Current version this lab quotes: 2025-11-25. [cite:9]
09Lab
No API key. A sheet of paper is enough. The scenario drills include the annotation case and the refund the policy forbids.

title: RAG end to end
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation, in the system you will actually ship, is a pipeline: chunk a corpus, embed it with one model, search, pack a few passages into the prompt, and require the language model to answer from those passages or abstain. The 2020 paper that named RAG is a related but stricter thing: a seq2seq model and a dense index trained so the generator is marginalized over retrieved documents. This room keeps those two meanings apart and walks the production path from document to cited answer.

blocks.title: Verification
blocks.text: Source note: last-verified was left unmarked until a person checks the cited pages. The citation list in this lesson keeps the page and the fetch date.

Retrieval-augmented generation, in the system you will actually ship, is a pipeline: chunk a corpus, embed it with one model, search, pack a few passages into the prompt, and require the language model to answer from those passages or abstain. The 2020 paper that named RAG is a related but stricter thing: a seq2seq model and a dense index trained so the generator is marginalized over retrieved documents. This room keeps those two meanings apart and walks the production path from document to cited answer.
01Executive summary

items: The paper (Lewis et al., NeurIPS 2020) combines a parametric seq2seq model with a non-parametric dense index of Wikipedia. The generator is BART-large. The retriever is initialized from Dense Passage Retrieval, a bi-encoder. They marginalize retrieved documents either once per output sequence (RAG-Sequence) or per token (RAG-Token). [cite:1]

What teams mean by RAG in 2026 is usually retrieve-then-read: a frozen chat model, an embeddings API, a vector index, and a prompt that says to use the retrieved text and to abstain otherwise. OpenAI’s embeddings guide demonstrates that shape: embed, rank by cosine similarity, and answer from the supplied article or say you do not know. [cite:2]

Query vectors and document vectors must come from the same embedding model. OpenAI documents default widths of 1536 and 3072 for two third-generation models and a `dimensions` parameter to shorten them. The embeddings API reference caps each input at 8192 tokens. [cite:2] [cite:3]

pgvector stores vectors in Postgres. Cosine distance is the `<=>` operator. Cosine similarity is one minus that distance. An HNSW index for cosine uses `vector_cosine_ops`. Hybrid search, in that README, means using Postgres full-text search as well and combining ranks with reciprocal rank fusion or a cross-encoder. [cite:4]

A fluent answer with no retrieved id in the trace is not grounded. The index can be replaced when facts change — that is the paper’s point about non-parametric memory — but only if you re-embed with the same model and you stop serving stale chunks. [cite:1]

blocks.title: Why it matters for the lab engineer
blocks.text: The grounded-assistant interview is this room drawn on a whiteboard: corpus, chunk, embed, filter, pack, cite, abstain, eval. Contact-center agent assist is the same pipeline pointed at a knowledge article and a CRM note, with the extra rule that the article’s license and the caller’s identity decide what may be retrieved. If you conflate the 2020 training recipe with a LangChain tutorial, a senior interviewer will notice. This room gives you the vocabulary to keep them separate.
02Architecture
Production path. Ingest is steps 1–4. Query is steps 5–7. Numbers match the walk-through.
Diagram: Documents, chunks, embed, index, query, pack, answer

items: 1–4 run when the corpus changes, not on every question.
5 must use the embedding model id stored with the index.
6 is a pack with ids, not a dump of the top fifty chunks.
7 either cites those ids or abstains. A third behavior — inventing — is a failure.

blocks.text: Mermaid source for a later redraw

flowchart TB
  subgraph ingest [Ingest]
    D[Documents] --> C[Chunks with ids]
    C --> E[Embed]
    E --> I[Index plus metadata]
  end
  Q[Question] --> EQ[Embed with the same model]
  EQ --> S[Top-k and filter]
  I --> S
  S --> P[Pack under a token budget]
  P --> L[Frozen chat model]
  L --> A[Cited answer or abstain]

The paper’s diagram is different. There the retriever is a probabilistic component p(z|x), the generator is a seq2seq model conditioned on a latent document, and training marginalizes that latent with a top-k approximation. You do not need to reproduce that training loop to ship retrieve-then-read. You do need to know it exists so you do not cite “RAG” and describe the wrong system. [cite:1]
03Deep dive

T1 established that a language model scores next tokens from whatever ids are in the window. RAG, in production, is how a specific paragraph gets into that window on purpose, with an id you can show later. If the paragraph never arrives, the model is back to parametric memory: fluent, and free to be wrong. The 2020 paper uses those words. Parametric memory is the generator’s weights. Non-parametric memory is the dense index. They showed you can replace the index to update what the system knows. [cite:1]

The generation model and the embedding model are different ids. The retrieval lesson does not depend on which generation id a vendor’s sample happens to print. OpenAI’s text guide, retrieved 2026-10-14, says the Responses `output` array can contain tool calls, not only text, and its code samples print `model: "gpt-6-astra"`. That string is an example on the page that day. A tool result that carries a retrieved passage is untrusted input, the same way a packed chunk is. MCP revision 2025-11-25 adds Resources as a server feature for context and data. That does not move the filter into the model. The host still decides which passages are allowed for this caller before anything is packed. [cite:13] [cite:14]
What the paper actually built

Lewis and co-authors treat the retrieved document as a latent variable. RAG-Sequence uses the same retrieved document for every token of the output. RAG-Token may use a different document for each output token. In both cases they approximate the sum over documents by the top k from the retriever. For RAG-Sequence the sequence probability is a sum, over those documents, of retriever probability times the full sequence probability under the generator. For RAG-Token the next-token probability is itself a sum over documents, and the sequence probability is the product of those mixtures. When the target is a single class label, the two formulas coincide because the sequence has length one. [cite:1]

The retriever is DPR: a query encoder and a document encoder, both initialized from BERT base in their description, scoring documents by inner product. Finding the top documents is maximum inner-product search. They initialize from a DPR checkpoint trained to retrieve passages that contain answers to TriviaQA and Natural Questions. The generator is BART-large, which they describe as a pretrained seq2seq transformer with 400 million parameters. Input and retrieved text are concatenated. They fine-tune the query encoder and BART. They keep the document encoder and the index fixed, because rebuilding the index whenever the document encoder moves is expensive, and they report they did not need that step for strong results. [cite:1]

Those are historical design choices. BART-large’s 400 million parameters are not the size of a 2026 chat model. The Wikipedia index is not your help center. The paper’s reported gains on Natural Questions, WebQuestions, and CuratedTrec are 2020 results. Cite them as the paper’s claims, not as a promise about your corpus. [cite:1]
Two systems people call RAG

rows: BART-large, fine-tuned, 400M parameters as stated in the paper. [cite:1]
A frozen chat model behind an API. Weights do not move when you add a document.
DPR bi-encoder, query encoder fine-tuned jointly, document encoder frozen. [cite:1]
An embedding model you call, then nearest neighbor. OpenAI’s guide ranks by cosine similarity. [cite:2]
Marginal likelihood of the target text. No direct label of which document was correct. [cite:1]
None inside the loop. You may later evaluate with a golden set (T5). That is not the paper’s loss.
Concatenated with the input inside the seq2seq model. [cite:1]
Placed in the prompt, with an instruction to use it or abstain. The embeddings guide shows that instruction on a short article. [cite:2]
Re-chunk, re-embed with the same model, swap the rows. A new chat model id does not require a re-embed. A new embedding model id does.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: In an interview, say which one you mean in the first sentence. “I am describing retrieve-then-read with a frozen generator, not the 2020 end-to-end marginalization, unless you want that paper.” Then draw ingest and query as two clocks.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: Switching from `text-embedding-3-small` to `text-embedding-3-large`, or shortening dimensions on one side only, puts queries and documents in different spaces. Neighbors become noise. The guide’s default widths are 1536 and 3072, and shortening is an explicit `dimensions` argument on third-generation models. Store the model id and the dimension next to every vector. [cite:2]
The production objects

headers: What goes wrong if you skip it
rows: A stable document id, a version or hash, and the license or audience. This room does not name that license. Record the one the content owner gave you.
You cannot delete a stale article, and you cannot prove you were allowed to send it to a model vendor.
Chunk id, document id, ordinal, the text, and the heading path that located it.
The model cites “the document” and a human cannot find the sentence.
The vector, the embedding model id, and the dimension.
A later query uses a different model and you do not notice until answers rot.
Fields you are willing to constrain: product, locale, effective date, audience.
The nearest neighbor is a paragraph from another country or last year’s policy.
The ordered chunk ids actually sent, and the token count of the pack.
The trace cannot explain the answer. An eval cannot compute recall of the gold chunk.
The string or structured flag you emit when no chunk supports an answer.
The model fills the gap from parametric memory and sounds sure.

blocks.text: Embeddings, cosine, and the index

OpenAI’s embeddings guide says to embed the query and each document and rank by cosine similarity. It recommends cosine similarity and says the choice of distance typically does not matter much. It also says third-generation vectors can be shortened with `dimensions`. Their guide claims that a `text-embedding-3-large` vector shortened to 256 still outperformed an unshortened `text-embedding-ada-002` vector of length 1536 on MTEB. That is their benchmark claim, tied to that write-up. It is not a promise about your help center. [cite:2]

The embeddings API reference lists models including `text-embedding-ada-002`, `text-embedding-3-small`, and `text-embedding-3-large`. It states a maximum of 8192 tokens per input for those embedding models, and it rejects an empty string. `dimensions` is supported on text-embedding-3 and later. [cite:3] A chunker that emits a chunk over 8192 tokens cannot embed it on that API without splitting again. As of 2026-10-14, OpenAI’s models page lists a 1.05M-token context window and a 128K max output for gpt-6-astra, gpt-6.1-sol, and gpt-6-luna. [cite:6]

pgvector’s README defines the operators: `<->` is L2 distance, `<#>` is negative inner product, `<=>` is cosine distance, `<+>` is L1. Cosine similarity is one minus cosine distance. An HNSW index that supports cosine ordering is created with `vector_cosine_ops`. The same README says to use full-text search alongside vectors for hybrid search, and to combine results with reciprocal rank fusion or a cross-encoder. It does not, in that section, lock the fusion constant. The README does not lock a fusion constant, so there is no official default to copy. Pick one, write it down, and test recall. [cite:4]

Order by distance ascending if the operator is a distance. Ordering by `<=>` descending ranks the worst neighbors first. That single sort direction is a common reason a demo “retrieves” irrelevant text while the vectors are fine.
A toy neighbor, so the metric is real

These are not model outputs. They are two-dimensional vectors chosen so the arithmetic fits on a page. Query q = [0.85, 0.15]. Chunk A = [0.90, 0.10]. Chunk B = [0.20, 0.80]. Cosine is the dot product divided by the product of the Euclidean norms.

Norm of q is the square root of 0.85² + 0.15², about 0.863. Norm of A is about 0.906. Dot product is 0.85×0.90 + 0.15×0.10 = 0.780. Cosine is about 0.780 / (0.863 × 0.906) ≈ 0.997. Norm of B is about 0.825. Dot product is 0.85×0.20 + 0.15×0.80 = 0.290. Cosine is about 0.290 / (0.863 × 0.825) ≈ 0.407. A is the neighbor. In pgvector, cosine distance to A is about 1 − 0.997 = 0.003, and to B about 0.593. `ORDER BY embedding <=> q LIMIT 1` returns A. [cite:4]
Toy cosines. Not an embedding model. The gap is the whole lesson: the outage-shaped vector beats the billing-shaped vector.

A real embedding model does this in hundreds or thousands of dimensions, and the gap is often much smaller. The operators do not change. What changes is that you must measure recall on your questions instead of trusting a two-dimensional drawing. Neither the pgvector README nor the OpenAI embeddings guide states a universal chunk size. Overlap between chunks is a knob you justify with a recall test, not a folklore fraction.
Packing and abstention

The embeddings guide’s question-answering sketch puts an article in the prompt and tells the model to answer from it, and to say it does not know when the answer is not there. One of the published snippets uses a short Winter Olympics sentence and the instruction to write that you do not know if the answer cannot be found. [cite:2] That is the behavior you want from step 7. Generalize it: label each chunk with its id, tell the model to cite those ids, and treat any claim without an id as a defect.

How many chunks fit is a token budget, which depends on the chat model’s window. As of 2026-10-14, OpenAI’s models page lists a 1.05M-token context window and a 128K max output for gpt-6-astra, gpt-6.1-sol, and gpt-6-luna. [cite:6] Spend the budget on the instruction, the question, and the chunks, in that order of protection: if you must cut, cut the lowest-ranked chunk, not the abstention rule. A pack that crowds out the instruction is a prompt bug that looks like a retriever bug.

Citations the model prints are strings. They are grounded only if they are ids you actually packed. A model can emit a plausible id it was not given. The check is a set intersection, not a vibe. If the intersection is empty, you do not show the answer to a caller.
What this room will not pretend

embedding model id

blocks.text: Rerankers, graph RAG, and a full metric suite are later rooms (T3-R05, T3-R08, T3-R07, T5). This room’s end-to-end path is complete without them: lexical hybrid is named because pgvector’s README names it, and you may add it when proper nouns and error codes matter. Check the reranker’s own benchmark for latency and the vendor’s quota page for the plan you pay for. Both vary by model, region, and plan. Do not quote a recall number for “hybrid is always better.” The README does not say that. [cite:4]
Operators, so the SQL matches the metric

rows: Ascending. Similarity is 1 minus this value. [cite:4]
`<#>` returns the negative inner product, because Postgres index scans on these operators are ascending
Ascending on that negative value ranks larger inner products first. The README says to multiply by −1 to recover the inner product. [cite:4]

blocks.text: The cosine row is the one this room’s lab uses, because the OpenAI embeddings guide recommends cosine and the pgvector README shows the matching operator and HNSW class. The other rows are the same README’s operators and the HNSW classes it prints beside them: `vector_l2_ops`, `vector_ip_ops`, `vector_cosine_ops`, and `vector_l1_ops`. Hamming and Jaccard are in that README for binary vectors and are out of scope for this pilot. [cite:2] [cite:4]
04Walk-through
Query time. Ingest has already stored vectors. Steps match the table.
Diagram: Sequence from user to app to embedding API to vector database to the language model

Question: “When did the overnight outage end?” Corpus: three chunks. A states the outage window. B states a billing rule. C tells the caller to press 0. The correct pack contains A and not a novel. The correct answer cites A’s id or abstains. It does not invent a minute.

rows: Keep document id and hash. Splitting rules are yours to test. Check a probe on your corpus. A useful length varies with the document and the embedding model.
Chunk text, non-empty, within 8192 tokens on OpenAI’s embedding models
Empty string is rejected. Record model id and dimensions. [cite:3]
Vector plus chunk id, document id, metadata
If the store is pgvector, build the index with the operator class you will query. Cosine needs `vector_cosine_ops`. [cite:4]
The question, plus audience and locale if you filter on them

A contact-center caller also has a queue and an authenticated identity. Do not retrieve another customer’s notes. Check the CRM’s field list for the object you filter on. Names differ by product and by tenant customization.
The question, same model id and dimension as step 2
Cosine is the guide’s recommendation for ranking those vectors. [cite:2]
Order by cosine distance ascending. k is a knob. Check a recall probe on your set. A useful k varies with corpus size and how sharp the neighbors are.
Instruction, question, labeled chunks, token budget
Instruction: answer only from these ids, cite them, otherwise abstain. Pattern from the embeddings guide’s article prompt. [cite:2] Sampling: one knob, per T1. [cite:5]
Text plus the ids it claims
Intersect claimed ids with packed ids. On empty intersection or abstention, do not present a fact.
Model ids, packed ids, scores, abstain bit, token usage

Without packed ids, T5 cannot grade faithfulness. Embedding prices on the OpenAI pricing page, as of 2026-10-14, are $0.02 per 1M tokens for text-embedding-3-small, $0.13 for text-embedding-3-large, and $0.10 for text-embedding-ada-002. [cite:7]

blocks.text: 05Config path

The admin path is a schema and a request, not a Control Hub wizard. The contact center still chooses when this retriever is allowed to run: a Webex flow, a UCCE script node, or a desktop gadget. Check the admin guide for the product version that starts the retriever. Click paths differ by product and release. The steps below are the retrieval service.

items: Pick one embedding model id and one dimension. Write them in config, not in a comment. OpenAI defaults cited above if you use that API. [cite:2]

Create the table: chunk id, document id, text, metadata, vector. The pgvector README’s examples declare the column as `embedding vector(3)`, and a later section says you can use the type `vector` instead of `vector(n)`. Use the width of the embedding model you actually call. The extension version installed on your server is still a separate check. [cite:4]
Create the index with the operator class that matches the query. For cosine, `hnsw` and `vector_cosine_ops`. [cite:4]
Ingest with a non-empty chunk under the embedding token cap. Store the document hash. [cite:3]
Query with a filter before you admire the score. A high cosine on the wrong audience is a defect.
Build the pack with ids in the text the model sees, and keep the same ids in the trace.
Set the chat instruction to the abstention pattern. The chat reference recommends altering temperature or top_p, but not both. It does not forbid sending both. [cite:2] [cite:5]
Reject answers whose cited ids are not a subset of the packed ids. Log the rejection.

blocks.title: Index drift
blocks.text: An HNSW index built for cosine will not serve an L2 ordering. The README’s operator and operator class have to match. If a query suddenly sequential-scans, this mismatch is the first check. [cite:4]

Query model id or dimension differs from the stored vectors
Config versus the column you stored at ingest
Re-embed the corpus with the new id, or roll the query back. Do not mix. [cite:2]

Metadata filter, wrong distance direction, or the HNSW operator class does not match the ORDER BY
Run the query without the filter. Check `<=>` versus `<->`. Explain the plan.
Align operator and operator class. Order distances ascending. [cite:4]

Packed ids in the trace. Temperature and top_p. Whether both were set.

Discard the answer. Tighten the instruction. This is not a cue to raise temperature.
Parametric memory filled the gap. Abstention did not fire.

Hard-stop in application code when the set is empty. Do not rely on the model to remember the rule. [cite:1]

blocks.text: 08Self-question ladder
L0 · What is RAG?

In this lab, RAG means putting retrieved source text into the model’s context so the answer can be tied to those sources. The 2020 paper means a specific probabilistic model that marginalizes a latent document. Say which one you mean. [cite:1]
L1 · Why retrieve if the model already generates fluent answers?

Fluency is not provenance, and weights do not update when a policy PDF changes. The paper calls out limited precise access to knowledge, missing provenance, and the difficulty of updating world knowledge, and it shows a non-parametric index you can replace. [cite:1]
L2 · How does a question become a cited answer, end to end?

Ingest: chunk, embed with a pinned model, store vector plus ids. Query: embed the question with that same model, take top-k under a metadata filter, pack the texts with their ids, ask a frozen model to answer only from them or abstain, then intersect cited ids with packed ids. [cite:2] [cite:4]
L2 · Where does the 2020 paper differ on that path?

The paper fine-tunes BART-large and the query encoder, freezes the document encoder, and marginalizes documents with RAG-Sequence or RAG-Token. It does not call a frozen chat API and it does not use cosine on OpenAI vectors. [cite:1]
L3 · The answer is wrong. How do I prove which stage failed?

Look at the trace in order. Was the gold chunk in the index? Did the filter remove it? Did top-k include it? Did the pack include it? Did the model cite it? Did application code accept a citation that was not packed? The first “no” is the stage. A wrong answer with an empty retrieved set is abstention failure, not a bad cosine. [cite:1]
L3 · What single query tells me the index is innocent?

Embed the gold chunk’s text and the question with the stored model id and compute cosine, or run the SQL with the filter removed. If the gold chunk ranks first in SQL and the bot still misses it, the bug is after retrieval: pack, prompt, or the string the bot actually embedded. [cite:4]
L4 · How does this differ across pgvector and a hosted vector service, and across model vendors?

The pipeline does not change: same embedding model on both sides, a filter, a pack, an abstention check. pgvector’s operators and HNSW operator classes are cited. As of 2026-10-14, Pinecone’s database-limits overview separates rate, object, operation, and identifier limits by plan and says many can be raised. Read that page for the plan you buy. Filtering syntax for a hosted service is that service’s page. [cite:8] OpenAI’s cosine recommendation is for their embeddings guide, not a law of every vendor. If another vendor’s model card demands inner product, follow the card. [cite:2] [cite:4]
L4 · How does retrieval sit on a Webex or UCCE assist desktop?

The phone system still owns the call. The retriever runs on the transcript so far, or on the agent’s question, and the pack must be allowed for that caller and that queue. Screen-pop of a cited article is a UI action. Transfer is still a route. This room does not name that gadget. The retrieval math does not become SIP.
L5 · If I redesigned this pipeline, what would I change, and what stops me?

I would store the rendered pack and the scores as first-class records, refuse uncited claims in code rather than in a prompt, and re-embed automatically when the embedding model id changes. What stops a casual redesign is the token budget of the chat model, the license to send corpus text to the embedding vendor, and the cost of rebuilding the index. As of 2026-10-14, OpenAI’s models page lists a 1.05M-token context window and a 128K max output for gpt-6-astra, gpt-6.1-sol, and gpt-6-luna. Embedding prices as of 2026-10-14 are on the pricing page cited here. The license to send a given corpus is still the content owner’s contract. [cite:6] [cite:7] The paper already shows the expensive version of an index rebuild: they froze the document encoder to avoid it. [cite:1]
L5 · What does a better chat model not fix?
A missing filter, a mixed embedding space, or a stale row. A stronger generator is more convincing when it fills a gap. The abstain check has to sit in your process. [cite:2]
Leaf · Why is cosine similarity one minus pgvector’s cosine operator?
The README defines `<=>` as cosine distance and tells you to subtract it from 1 to get similarity. You sort the distance ascending to get the nearest neighbor. [cite:4]
Leaf · What did RAG-Token change relative to RAG-Sequence?
RAG-Token can assign a different latent document to each output token. RAG-Sequence uses one document for the whole sequence. They match when the output length is one. [cite:1]
Leaf · When do I reach for hybrid search?

When the question is a rare string — an error code, a SKU, a proper noun — and vector neighbors miss the gold chunk that full-text search would hit. The README names the combination and names RRF or a cross-encoder as the fuse. It does not give you a recall guarantee. [cite:4]
09Lab

items: Goal: by hand, rank two toy chunks for one query with cosine, write the pgvector order-by that returns the winner, and draft a four-line pack that forces a citation or an abstention.
Prerequisites: T1-R01 lab completed on paper. Postgres is optional. An API key is optional. Do not ingest a real customer corpus. Any sample text you embed must be yours.
Step 1. Compute cosine for q=[0.85, 0.15], A=[0.90, 0.10], B=[0.20, 0.80]. Expected: A near 0.997, B near 0.407.
Step 2. Convert both to cosine distance with 1 − cosine. Expected: A near 0.003, B near 0.593. Write `ORDER BY embedding <=> q LIMIT 1` and say which row returns. [cite:4]

Step 3. Write a pack: an instruction to answer only from the labeled chunks or say “I don’t know,” chunk A with id `outage-14`, and the question about when the outage ended. Expected shape matches the embeddings guide’s “use the article / say you don’t know” pattern. [cite:2]
Step 4. Invent a bad model reply that cites `outage-99`. Apply the intersection check. Expected: reject.
Step 5. State whether your exercise was paper RAG or retrieve-then-read, in one sentence. Expected: retrieve-then-read. You did not marginalize a latent document or fine-tune BART.
Evidence: the arithmetic, the SQL fragment, the pack, and the rejected reply, on one page in your private notes.

Break-it: swap in a query vector from a “different model” by using [0.20, 0.80] as the query while pretending the index was built with the original embedding. Expected: B wins for the wrong reason. Recovery: refuse to query until model id and dimension match the index. [cite:2]

Optional: if you already run Postgres with pgvector, create a two-row table and the HNSW cosine index from the README and confirm the plan uses the index. Match the README at the commit you installed. This room does not copy a second syntax. [cite:4]
Reflection: where did you almost trust a fluent sentence that failed the id intersection?

blocks.text: 10Quiz
Multiple choice
Q1. In the 2020 paper, non-parametric memory is:

items: The BART weights.
The dense vector index of documents.
The softmax temperature.
The chat template.

blocks.text: Reveal
B. Parametric memory is the generator. [cite:1]
Multiple choice
Q2. RAG-Sequence differs from RAG-Token because:

items: Only RAG-Token uses a retriever.
RAG-Sequence conditions the whole output on one retrieved document; RAG-Token may switch document per token.
RAG-Sequence is cosine search.
They are the same for every sequence length.

blocks.text: Reveal
B. They coincide for a length-one target. [cite:1]
Multiple choice
Q3. OpenAI’s embeddings guide tells you to rank documents by:

items: Edit distance on the raw strings.
Cosine similarity of embedding vectors.
BLEU against the query.
The chat model’s attention map.

blocks.text: Reveal
B. [cite:2]
Multiple choice
Q4. pgvector’s cosine distance operator is:
Reveal
C. L2 is `<->`, negative inner product is `<#>`, L1 is `<+>`. Similarity is 1 minus cosine distance. [cite:4]
Multiple choice
Q5. Default vector length for text-embedding-3-large in the guide is:
Reveal
C. 1536 is the small model’s default. 8192 is the per-input token cap, not the width. 256 is an example of shortening. [cite:2] [cite:3]
Scenario
Q6. You change only the query to text-embedding-3-large and leave last month’s small-model index in place. What happens?
Reveal

You search across incompatible vectors. Re-embed or revert. The guide’s two defaults are different widths, which makes the mismatch obvious, and even equal widths would not make different models comparable. [cite:2]
Scenario
Q7. Top-1 is the gold chunk. The spoken answer states a different time and cites no id. Where is the bug?
Reveal

After retrieval: pack, instruction, or the application’s willingness to show an uncited claim. Do not rebuild the index first. The abstention pattern belongs in the prompt and the empty-citation check belongs in code. [cite:2]
Scenario
Q8. A caller with no authentication receives another account’s balance sentence. What failed?
Reveal
The metadata filter, or the decision to retrieve at all. Ranking quality is irrelevant. Stop the path. This room does not name the CRM field. The control is not optional.
Draw it
Q9. Draw ingest and query as two separate timelines and mark the only arrow that must use the same model id.
Reveal

Ingest: document → chunk → embed → index. Query: question → embed → search → pack → generate → check ids. The two embed steps share the model id and the dimension. The chat model id may differ. [cite:2]
Draw it
Q10. Sketch RAG-Sequence versus RAG-Token for a three-token answer and two documents.
Reveal
Sequence: one document choice covers all three tokens. Token: each of the three positions may pick either document, and the probability mixes inside the product. [cite:1]
Short answer
Q11. The paper froze which encoder, and why?
Reveal
The document encoder, and the index built from it, because updating it means rebuilding the index. They fine-tuned the query encoder and BART. [cite:1]
Short answer
Q12. What does the embeddings guide say to do when the article does not contain the answer?
Reveal
Say you do not know. The published sketch uses that instruction rather than asking the model to improvise. [cite:2]
Short answer
Q13. Which column types does the pgvector README show for a 3-dimensional embedding?
Reveal

The examples use `vector(3)`. A later section says you may store the column as `vector` without a fixed width, and cast to `vector(3)` when you index or order. The width still has to match the model. [cite:4]
Scenario
Q14. Recall of the gold chunk fell after you re-embedded with a new model id but kept the old index. What is the first repair?
Reveal

Rebuild the index with the same embedding model that embeds the query. Mixing widths or models makes cosine a comparison of unlike spaces. Do not “fix” it by raising k until the old vectors happen to look close. [cite:2] [cite:4]

The player loads a local silent placeholder. Studio replaces the takes.

title: Vector databases and hybrid search
summary: pgvector stores vectors in Postgres and can index them with HNSW or IVFFlat. BM25 is a lexical score, and Elasticsearch documents it as the default similarity. Reciprocal rank fusion combines ranked lists. This room keeps those three mechanisms in separate sentences so a design review cannot pretend one extension does all three.

blocks.title: Verification
blocks.text: Source note: last-verified was left unmarked until a person checks the cited pages. The citation list in this lesson keeps the page and the fetch date.

pgvector stores vectors in Postgres and can index them with HNSW or IVFFlat. BM25 is a lexical score, and Elasticsearch documents it as the default similarity. Reciprocal rank fusion combines ranked lists. This room keeps those three mechanisms in separate sentences so a design review cannot pretend one extension does all three.
01Executive summary

items: pgvector’s HNSW index is a multilayer graph. The README says it has better query speed-recall than IVFFlat, builds more slowly, and uses more memory. You can create it on an empty table. IVFFlat divides vectors into lists and searches the lists closest to the query. It builds faster, uses less memory, and needs data before you create the index because it trains. [cite:1]

Filtering on those approximate indexes is applied after the index scan. Since 0.8.0, iterative scans can keep looking. The README’s examples set hnsw.ef_search, ivfflat.probes, and the iterative-scan modes. Those are starting points, not a universal production setting. [cite:1]

BM25 is Elasticsearch’s default similarity. The 8.19 reference documents k1 default 1.2, b default 0.75, and discount_overlaps default true. pgvector does not implement BM25. Postgres full-text search is a different feature, tsvector and ts_rank. Do not write a sentence that says the extension “does hybrid BM25.” [cite:2]

Elasticsearch’s RRF retriever defaults rank_constant to 60, and the constant must be at least 1. A higher constant gives lower-ranked documents more influence. The 8.19 guide’s rank_window_size defaults to 10 and must be at least the requested size. The page names combining a standard retriever with a knn or ELSER retriever as a primary use. The pgvector README mentions reciprocal rank fusion as one way to fuse full-text and vectors and does not lock the constant. [cite:3] [cite:1]

Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, Milvus, and Chroma are names of products. Check that vendor’s limits page for the plan you pay for. Pod size and payload caps vary by vendor, plan, and region, which is why a remembered number does not belong here.

blocks.title: Why it matters for the lab engineer
blocks.text: A contact-center bot that misses “refund policy” when the caller says “you owe me money back” is often a vector neighbor that never shared those words, or a lexical hit that never shared the embedding. Hybrid search is how you stop choosing only one failure. It is not a license to mix embedding models, skip the filter, or quote a rank constant you did not write down. The caller hears one answer. You should be able to say which list it came from.
02Architecture
Two lists, one fusion. Vectors and lexical ranks stay separate until a documented combiner.
Diagram: Seven stages: chunks, embed, HNSW or IVFFlat, lexical BM25 or tsvector, fuse with RRF, filter, pack

items: 1–3 are the vector path. The index type is HNSW or IVFFlat, not both on the same column unless you built two indexes on purpose.
4 is lexical. In Elasticsearch that default is BM25. In Postgres it is full-text search, not a pgvector operator.
5 fuses ranks. 6 is the metadata filter. 7 packs text for the model or abstains.

blocks.text: Sequence: the application asks both indexes, then fuses, then packs.
Diagram: App, Postgres vector index, lexical index, fusion step, and the packer that labels untrusted text

The picture does not include a reranker. A cross-encoder over the fused list is the next room’s problem, and it can only reorder what fusion already returned. If both lists missed the gold chunk, fusion cannot invent it.
03Deep dive

T3-R01 already fixed the operators. Cosine distance is `<=>`, L2 is `<->`, negative inner product is `<#>`, L1 is `<+>`. The query vector and the stored vectors come from the same embedding model. This room starts where that room stopped: which index structure you build, what a lexical score is, and how two ranked lists become one. [cite:1]
HNSW in the README

HNSW builds a multilayer graph. The README’s claim against IVFFlat is better speed-recall at query time, a slower build, and more memory. Because there is no training step, you may create the index on an empty table and insert later. The create statement in the README looks like `CREATE INDEX ... USING hnsw (embedding vector_l2_ops)`, and the same pattern exists for `vector_ip_ops`, `vector_cosine_ops`, and `vector_l1_ops`. Bit vectors have `bit_hamming_ops` and `bit_jaccard_ops`. Build parameters in the example are `m = 16` and `ef_construction = 64`. At query time the example is `SET hnsw.ef_search = 100`, and `SET LOCAL` works inside a transaction. The filtering section mentions a default `hnsw.ef_search` of 40: if a filter matches 10 percent of rows, only about 4 rows match on average. That sentence is an illustration of post-filtering, not a recommendation to leave the default untouched. [cite:1]

A notice you should expect on a large build says the HNSW graph no longer fits in `maintenance_work_mem` after 100000 tuples. That is the README’s notice text. It is a memory fact about the build, not a statement that 100000 is the largest legal index. Raise the memory setting if you intend to build past it, and still measure recall on your questions. Do not treat the notice as a capacity plan for a contact center.
IVFFlat in the README

IVFFlat splits vectors into lists and searches the lists closest to the query. The README says the build is faster and the index uses less memory than HNSW, with lower query performance. You need rows first. The index trains on them. Starting points printed in the README: set `lists` to rows divided by 1000 for up to a million rows, and to the square root of the row count above a million rows. Start `probes` at the square root of `lists`. The example uses `lists = 100` and `SET ivfflat.probes = 10`. If probes equals the number of lists, the search is exact nearest neighbor and the planner may ignore the index. Those are starting points. A production contact-center index is whatever recall you measured, not the example’s 100. [cite:1]

blocks.title: The filter happens after the approximate scan
blocks.text: The README says filtering on approximate indexes is applied after the index scan. If you ask for the nearest refund article inside one product line, the graph may return neighbors from other products and the filter may then discard them, leaving you with too few rows. Iterative scans, since version 0.8.0, exist for that case. `hnsw.iterative_scan` can be `strict_order` or `relaxed_order`. IVFFlat’s iterative scan in the README is `relaxed_order`. They stop at `hnsw.max_scan_tuples` or `ivfflat.max_probes`. The example max scan tuples is 20000. A partial index, `WHERE (category_id = 123)`, is the other tool when the predicate is stable. [cite:1]
BM25 is not a pgvector operator

Elasticsearch documents BM25 as the default similarity. k1 defaults to 1.2 and controls term-frequency saturation. b defaults to 0.75 and controls length normalization. discount_overlaps defaults to true. You can cite those three defaults from the 8.19 index-modules page. You cannot cite them as pgvector settings, because they are not in the pgvector README. [cite:2]

Postgres can rank text with `tsvector` and `ts_rank`. That is full-text search in the database you already use for vectors. It is a reasonable lexical list to fuse with `<=>`. It is not BM25 unless you have installed something that implements BM25 and you have read that project’s docs. This room did not fetch a Postgres BM25 extension. If a teammate says “pgvector BM25,” correct the noun. The extension contributes the vector type and the vector indexes. The lexical score comes from elsewhere. [cite:1]

blocks.text: Reciprocal rank fusion

Elasticsearch’s RRF retriever combines two or more child retrievers. The 8.19 guide says rank_constant defaults to 60 and must be greater than or equal to 1. A higher constant gives lower-ranked documents more influence. rank_window_size defaults to 10 in that guide and must be at least 1 and at least the requested size. The primary use case named on the page is to combine BM25, via a standard retriever, with a knn retriever or an ELSER retriever. Later Elastic docs exist. This room pins the 8.19 page it fetched on 2026-10-14 and also points at the current REST page so you can see if the window default moved. If the two pages disagree when you re-fetch, the disagreement is the fact. Do not average them. [cite:3] [cite:4]

The pgvector README’s hybrid sentence is shorter. It says you can combine full-text search with vectors using reciprocal rank fusion or a cross-encoder. It does not print 60. If you implement fusion in SQL, write the constant in the query or the config, and test recall. Copying Elastic’s 60 into Postgres is a choice you document, not a default Postgres shipped. A cross-encoder is a second model that reads a short list. It is not RRF. RRF never opens the text. It only trusts the ranks the two lists already produced.

blocks.title: Write the constant down
blocks.text: A recall change after “we turned on hybrid” is unreadable if nobody recorded rank_constant, the lexical analyzer, the embedding model id, and ef_search or probes. The incident review will relitigate folklore. The record is four numbers and two model strings.
What this room will not invent

Hosted vector databases differ in tenancy, filtering, and payload limits. Pass 3 already failed to fetch several of those child pages cleanly. This pass does not fill the gap from memory. If you need a Pinecone pod size, a Qdrant payload cap, or a Weaviate class limit, open that vendor’s page and cite it, then drop any mark. Until that fetch, the comparison you are allowed to teach is the one above: pgvector’s two index types, Elasticsearch’s BM25 defaults, and Elasticsearch’s RRF defaults. Chroma and Milvus can sit in the ecosystem table as names. They do not sit in the limits table as numbers.

Same-model discipline survives hybrid search. A lexical hit does not repair a query vector from text-embedding-3-large scored against a column of text-embedding-3-small. OpenAI’s guide, fetched 2026-10-14, defaults those widths at 1536 and 3072 and recommends cosine. Fusion will happily blend a nonsense vector ranking with a sensible BM25 ranking and still look “hybrid.” Check the model id before you celebrate the fused list. [cite:5]

OWASP LLM08 is the reminder that embeddings are an attack surface: poisoned documents, cross-tenant neighbors, and vectors that smuggle instructions. A metadata filter after the scan is not a complete tenant boundary if the approximate scan already mixed customers and the iterative scan then worked hard to find more of the wrong tenant. Partial indexes or a hard predicate the planner must respect belong in the design, and the security review belongs in T8. LLM01 still applies to whatever text you pack. Hybrid retrieval does not fully mitigate prompt injection. [cite:6]
Four queries, one index

Query A is the exact title “Refund policy.” BM25, or a tsvector of the title, should surface the page whose heading is those words. A pure vector search might prefer a paragraph that talks around refunds without using the heading. If you only ship vectors, you will file a bug against the embedding model for a lexical miss. Hybrid exists so the heading can win on rank even when the vector list preferred a paraphrase.

Query B is “you took my money twice,” with no shared keywords. The lexical list may return nothing useful. The vector list may return the double-charge article if the embedding space put those phrases near each other. Hybrid exists so a paraphrase is not punished for failing BM25. If the vector list is empty because the column was embedded with a different model, fusion will not save you. Rebuild, as T3-R01 already said.

Query C is “refund policy” plus a filter `product = voice` on a table that is mostly chat articles. HNSW returns approximate neighbors, then the filter discards them. You see three rows and blame recall. The README’s post-filter warning is this incident. Iterative scan or a partial index is the change. Raising temperature on the language model is not. [cite:1]

Query D is a tie: both lists return the gold article at different ranks, and a stale article ranks high on BM25 because the old heading still matches. RRF will blend the ranks. It will not know the document hash changed on Tuesday. Freshness is a filter or a sort on metadata you stored, not a property of k1. Record the hash at index time. T5 grades whether the packed id is the current id.

Across the four queries the lesson is which list failed. Log both ranks and the fused rank. A single “score” that already mixed them cannot be debugged at 2 a.m. Elasticsearch can return the child retrievers’ hits if you ask it to. Your SQL can return them because you wrote the query. Either way, store them on the trace next to `gen_ai.operation.name` when you mean retrieval. The OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions this lab pins are commit 4e8a281. [cite:7]
How to talk about scale without inventing a vendor

Scale, in this room, means the index still returns the gold chunk when the table is no longer a demo. The README already tells you the shape of that problem. HNSW’s graph wants memory, and the notice at 100000 tuples is the build telling you maintenance_work_mem is the first cliff, not the last. IVFFlat’s list count is a function of row count, so a table that grows from a hundred thousand rows to two million is not the same lists formula: below a million the README says rows/1000, above a million it says the square root. Recompute when you cross that line. Leaving lists at the example value of 100 because it was in the snippet is how a large table gets a toy index. [cite:1]

Query-time scale is ef_search or probes, and it is a recall-versus-latency knob you measure. The README does not publish a millisecond budget. A contact center that needs the first token inside a voice budget still measures that budget in T7. This room’s contribution is to refuse a number you did not time, and to put the index knob in the same trace as the model call so a slow pack is not blamed on the sampler. If probes is high enough that IVFFlat becomes exact, you may have purchased a sequential scan. EXPLAIN is the tool. A dashboard that only shows “vector p95” without the plan will call that scan a victory because the answers got more accurate and hide that the index was not used.

Hybrid scale has a second axis: the lexical window. Elasticsearch’s 8.19 RRF page defaults rank_window_size to 10. Ten documents is a small committee. A filter that already threw away most of a large corpus can make those ten the wrong ten. Raise the window on purpose, record it, and accept the cost. Do not raise it because a blog said 100, and do not leave it at 10 because the default felt official, if your recall set says the gold article was ranked 11th on one of the child lists. The child list’s rank is the evidence. The default is the starting point. [cite:3]

There is a third axis people skip because it is not an index parameter. Ingest rate. OpenAI’s rate-limits guide, fetched 2026-10-14, lists file ingest at 300 requests per minute per vector store id for that product’s vector stores. That number is not a pgvector setting and not an Elasticsearch bulk-thread count. It is a reminder that “scale” on a hosted embedding API is a quota on the Limits screen, while scale on your own HNSW build is memory and time. Quote the 300 only when you are talking about that OpenAI ingest path. [cite:9]

Tenant scale is the axis that becomes an incident. A single HNSW graph over every customer, with a product filter applied after the scan, will degrade exactly as the README’s 10-percent illustration predicts, and it will degrade worse when the tenant is one percent of the table. Iterative scan spends more work to fill the limit. A partial index per tenant spends disk to avoid the mix. Neither choice is free. The wrong choice is the one nobody wrote down, followed by a pack that contains another customer’s refund article. That defect is not a tuning anecdote. It is the reason LLM08 is on the OWASP list this lab already fetched. [cite:6]

When you present this to a design review, draw two boxes and a fuse, and put the numbers you will actually set under the boxes: operator class, m or lists, ef_search or probes, lexical engine, k1 and b if the engine is Elasticsearch, rank_constant, window, embedding model id, and the predicate. If a box says “Pinecone, 100 pods” and you cannot open the page, delete the box. The review can survive a missing vendor. It cannot survive a fabricated cap. The same rule keeps this room shorter than a market survey and more usable than one.

A worked fusion, so the constant is not a slogan: three articles, ranks starting at 1. Policy is lexical rank 1 and vector rank 5. Paraphrase is lexical rank 8 and vector rank 1. Stale heading is lexical rank 2 and vector rank 9. With rank_constant 60, a document’s fused score is the sum over lists of 1/(60+rank). Policy scores 1/61 plus 1/65. Paraphrase scores 1/68 plus 1/61. Stale scores 1/62 plus 1/69. You do not need a calculator to see that policy and paraphrase both sit near two sixtieths, and the stale article is close behind because lexical rank 2 is almost as strong as rank 1 when the constant is 60. That closeness is the point of a large constant: it stops a single first-place finish from erasing the other list. If you wanted the first place to dominate, you would lower the constant, document the change, and re-run the recall set. Elastic’s page says the higher constant gives lower-ranked documents more influence. The arithmetic above is how that sentence feels on three rows. It is not a proof that 60 is correct for your corpus. [cite:3]

Operators still matter on the vector side of that example. If you built the index with vector_l2_ops and you query with cosine distance, you are not testing fusion. You are testing a mismatch. The README’s operator classes are part of the create statement, not a hint you may ignore at query time. Cosine distance remains `<=>`, and similarity is one minus that distance. Order by the distance ascending if you want the nearest neighbor. A fused rank that used a similarity sorted backwards will look like “hybrid is random.” It is the ORDER BY. T3-R01’s operator table is still the law under this room’s indexes. [cite:1]

Bit vectors are the README’s other family, and they are easy to skip if you only embed floats. Hamming and Jaccard operator classes exist for bit columns. They are not a substitute for cosine on a float embedding, and they are not BM25. If a future design quantizes vectors to bits, cite the operator you built and measure recall again. Do not assume the float HNSW graph and the bit index rank the same neighbors. The README listing both is the permission to build them. It is not a claim that they agree. [cite:1]

Partial indexes deserve a last concrete picture. `WHERE (category_id = 123)` builds a graph that only contains that category. A query for category 123 can use it. A query for category 999 cannot, and should not fall through into someone else’s graph because the application forgot the predicate. Write the predicate in the application and in the index. Post-filtering is the safety net for predicates you cannot carve into the index. It is a weak net when the predicate is very selective, which is why iterative scan exists. Use the net. Prefer the carve when the predicate is stable. Say which one you shipped. [cite:1]
04Walk-through

blocks.text: 08Self-question ladder
Answer out loud. A leaf ends in a citation or a TODO-verify.
L0 · What does pgvector contribute to hybrid search?
The vector type and the approximate indexes, HNSW or IVFFlat, plus the distance operators. It does not contribute BM25. [cite:1]
L1 · When can you build HNSW on an empty table?
When you accept the README’s statement that HNSW has no training step. IVFFlat is the index that wants rows first. [cite:1]
L1 · What does the README say HNSW trades against IVFFlat?
Better query speed-recall, a slower build, and more memory. Those are the README’s comparisons, not your benchmark until you run one. [cite:1]
L2 · Why does a selective filter return too few HNSW hits?

Filtering is applied after the approximate index scan. With the default ef_search of 40 mentioned in that section, a filter that matches 10 percent of rows leaves about four hits on average. Iterative scan or a partial index is the documented response. [cite:1]
L2 · What is probes equal to lists?
Exact nearest neighbor for IVFFlat, and the planner may not use the index. [cite:1]
L3 · Quote Elasticsearch BM25 defaults.
k1 is 1.2, b is 0.75, discount_overlaps is true, on the 8.19 similarity page fetched 2026-10-14. [cite:2]
L3 · Is ts_rank the same citation?
No. Postgres full-text search was not given those k1 and b values in this room. Do not paste Elasticsearch defaults onto tsvector.
L3 · What is rank_constant 60?
The default on Elasticsearch’s RRF retriever. It must be at least 1. A higher constant gives lower-ranked documents more influence. The pgvector README does not lock this number. [cite:3] [cite:1]
L4 · What did the 8.19 guide say about rank_window_size?
It defaults to 10, and it must be at least 1 and at least the size you requested. Re-fetch the current REST page before you treat 10 as eternal. [cite:3] [cite:4]
L4 · Why log both child ranks?
Because a fused score hides which list failed. Query A in this room is a lexical win. Query B is a vector win. One number cannot tell them apart.
L5 · If you redesigned the index, what would you change, and what stops you?

I would partial-index by tenant and product before I raised ef_search, and I would record rank_constant in the same migration as the embedding model id. What stops a looser design is LLM08 and a pack that contains another customer’s article. Check the vendor’s limits page for the plan you pay for. Caps vary by vendor, plan, and region. [cite:6]
Leaf · Where does a cross-encoder sit?
After the fused list, on a short candidate set. It cannot recover a chunk both lists dropped. The README names it as an alternative to RRF, not as a synonym. [cite:1]
Leaf · What embedding widths are you not allowed to mix?
text-embedding-3-small defaults to 1536 and text-embedding-3-large to 3072 in OpenAI’s guide. Cosine is the recommended similarity. A hybrid lexical list does not excuse a mixed column. [cite:5]
Leaf · Which pgvector release introduced iterative scans?
0.8.0, as the README states. Modes named there include strict_order and relaxed_order for HNSW, and relaxed_order for IVFFlat. [cite:1]
09Lab
No database server is required. Paper or a local scratch query if you already have Postgres. Do not point this lab at a production cluster.

The framework does not choose HNSW versus IVFFlat for you in that sentence.

They do not choose m or k1. A wrong pack is a retrieval bug, not a voice-latency bug.

title: Agents and the Model Context Protocol
summary: An agent, in the sense this lab uses, is a loop: the model may request a tool, your process executes the tool, and the result goes back into the next model call until a stop rule fires. The Model Context Protocol is not that loop. It is a JSON-RPC contract so a host application can talk to many tool servers without inventing a plugin format each time. This room builds both, and it keeps the model from being the thing that runs your code.

blocks.title: Verification
blocks.text: Source note: last-verified was left unmarked until a person checks the cited pages. The citation list in this lesson keeps the page and the fetch date.

An agent, in the sense this lab uses, is a loop: the model may request a tool, your process executes the tool, and the result goes back into the next model call until a stop rule fires. The Model Context Protocol is not that loop. It is a JSON-RPC contract so a host application can talk to many tool servers without inventing a plugin format each time. This room builds both, and it keeps the model from being the thing that runs your code.
01Executive summary

items: ReAct (Yao et al., ICLR 2023) interleaves a natural-language reasoning trace with actions against an environment. On ALFWorld and WebShop the paper reports absolute success-rate gains of 34 and 10 points over imitation and reinforcement-learning baselines, with one or two in-context examples. Those are paper results, not your bot’s SLA. [cite:1]

OpenAI’s function-calling guide describes a five-step flow: send tools, receive a tool call, execute in your application, send the tool output back, receive a final answer or another call. The model does not run your function. The guide’s built-in tools include access to an MCP server, which is a product feature, not a substitute for reading the protocol. [cite:2]

Anthropic’s tool-use docs split client tools, which you execute after a `tool_use` block and a `stop_reason` of `tool_use`, from server tools Anthropic executes. A user-defined tool name must match `^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,64}$`. `tool_choice` has auto, any, tool, and none. [cite:3] [cite:4]

MCP specification 2025-11-25 defines hosts, clients, and servers over JSON-RPC 2.0. Servers offer resources, prompts, and tools. Clients may offer sampling, roots, and elicitation. Standard transports in that revision are stdio and Streamable HTTP. Streamable HTTP replaces the HTTP+SSE transport from the 2024-11-05 revision. [cite:5] [cite:6]

The spec’s security principles are normative for implementors even where the protocol cannot enforce them: explicit user consent, data minimization, treating tool descriptions as untrusted unless the server is trusted, and explicit approval before a tool runs or a sampling request is fulfilled. [cite:5]

blocks.title: Why it matters for the lab engineer
blocks.text: Agent interviews fail when the candidate says the model “called the API” and cannot say which process executed it. Contact-center interviews fail the same way: a transfer, a refund, or a screen-pop is a side effect a human or a tested function must own. MCP is how you attach those functions to more than one host without rewriting the plugin each time. This room is the oral answer and the sequence diagram.
02Architecture
Seven stages. The model sits inside the host. The tool sits behind the server. Consent sits on the arrow into the tool.
Diagram: User, host, MCP client, MCP server, tool, result, reply

items: 1 and 7 are the user. The user is not inside the server.
2 is the host: model loop, policy, and the decision to execute.
3–4 are the MCP session. A provider’s native tool JSON can replace this hop when you are not using MCP.
5 is your code. The model never is.

blocks.text: Mermaid source for a later redraw

flowchart LR
  U[User] --> H[Host and model loop]
  H --> C[MCP client]
  C --> S[MCP server]
  S --> T[Tool implementation]
  T --> S --> C --> H --> U

If you are not using MCP, delete boxes 3 and 4 and let the host speak the provider’s tool schema directly. The execution rule does not change. OpenAI and Anthropic both document that client-side tools run in your application. [cite:2] [cite:3]
03Deep dive

T1’s model emits tokens. Sometimes those tokens are not a sentence for the user. They are a structured request: a name and an argument object. T3’s retriever can be one such request. This room is the general case, plus the protocol that standardizes how a desktop, an IDE, or a contact-center orchestrator discovers those requests’ schemas.

Fetched 2026-10-14, OpenAI’s text guide says: “If you're building any text generation app, we recommend using the Responses API over the older Chat Completions API.” The same page says the `output` array can hold a tool call rather than a sentence, and its code samples print `model: "gpt-6-astra"`. Treat that id as the sample’s illustration. The pattern is Responses plus a snapshot pin you copy from the models page on the day you ship. The MCP specification this lab pins is revision 2025-11-25. It is JSON-RPC 2.0 among a host, a client inside the host, and a server. Servers may offer Resources, Prompts, and Tools. Clients may offer Sampling, Roots, and Elicitation. The same page says users must consent before a tool runs, and that tool descriptions are untrusted unless the server is trusted. The host still executes. A second model agreeing is not that consent. [cite:5] [cite:16]
What “agent” means here

The word is overloaded. In this lab an agent is not a person in a queue, and it is not a product brand. It is a control loop with a budget. The loop maintains a transcript. Each turn, the model either returns something you are willing to show the user, or returns one or more tool calls. Your code runs the calls, appends results, and asks the model again. The loop stops on a final answer, a budget (steps, tokens, or money), an error you refuse to retry, or a human rejection. A loop without a stop rule is not an agent. It is a bill.

ReAct is the paper that made the interleaved shape famous. The authors generate reasoning traces and task-specific actions together. The trace is there to update a plan and to handle exceptions. The action is there to pull information from outside the model, in their QA setup a Wikipedia API. They argue this reduces the hallucination and error propagation they associate with chain-of-thought alone, because the model can look something up instead of continuing from a bad premise. On HotpotQA and FEVER they use that API. On ALFWorld and WebShop they report absolute success gains of 34% and 10% against imitation and reinforcement-learning methods, prompted with one or two examples. The work was published at ICLR 2023. Cite the gains as the paper’s, on those benchmarks, with those backbones. Do not import them into a voice-bot slide. [cite:1]
Three layers you must not collapse

rows: The model, given the schemas and the transcript
A name and arguments. On Anthropic, a `tool_use` block. On OpenAI, a tool call your application executes. [cite:2] [cite:3]
You think “the model did the refund.” It did not. It requested one.
Allow, deny, or ask the user. MCP’s spec says hosts must obtain explicit consent before invoking a tool, and that tool descriptions are untrusted unless the server is trusted. [cite:5]
A poisoned tool description becomes an instruction to exfiltrate data. The model will follow schemas. Your policy has to be outside the schema.
Your function, a system of record, or — for Anthropic server tools — Anthropic’s infrastructure
A result or an error, tied to the call id
A retry without idempotency performs the side effect twice.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Say “the model requested `transfer_to_queue`” and “the host executed it after the caller confirmed.” The second sentence is the one a contact-center architect trusts. The first sentence alone is how you double-transfer someone.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: Anthropic documents that `tool_choice` of `any` or `tool` prefills the assistant message so the model does not emit natural language before the `tool_use` block, even if you asked it to explain first. If you need the explanation and the call, they tell you to stay on `auto` and put the instruction in the user message. Forcing a tool and expecting a preamble will confuse your parser. [cite:4]
Provider tool contracts you can quote

OpenAI’s guide walks a weather-style story and then generalizes. Tools are declared to the model. A tool call is the model’s request. A tool output is what your code returns, referenced by a call id. The five steps are request, tool call, execute, second request with the output, final response or more calls. With the Responses API the loop can continue. A function is one kind of tool, defined by a JSON schema. Custom tools take free text. Built-in tools cover web search, code execution, and MCP server access, among others named in that guide. [cite:2]

The same guide’s `tool_choice` list, as fetched for this room, includes auto (default: zero, one, or many), required (one or more), a forced function by name, and an `allowed_tools` restriction. You can also set `none`. Parallel function calls, on supported models beginning with GPT-5 in that guide’s wording, can happen alongside a constraint: built-in tools cannot sit in a parallel function-call batch. `parallel_tool_calls: false` limits a turn to zero or one tool. Tool search, which defers loading large catalogs, is documented for `gpt-5.4` and later. The guide also says GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol require the Responses API for tool calling, and that chat-completions examples there use GPT-5.6 Terra. Those are statements in the guide fetched on 2026-10-14. Confirm the id your key can call before you write it into a design. [cite:2]

Anthropic’s overview says tool use lets Claude call functions you define or tools Anthropic provides. Client tools return `stop_reason: "tool_use"` and one or more `tool_use` blocks. You execute and send `tool_result`. Server tools such as the ones named in that overview — the page lists web search, web fetch, code execution, and tool search — run on Anthropic’s side, with a caveat when they are mixed into a parallel batch with your client tools. Default `tool_choice` is auto: Claude calls a tool when the request maps to the tool and the answer is not already in context. The “how tool use works” page is explicit that the model does not execute your implementation. It sees the schema and the result you return. [cite:3]

A user-defined Anthropic tool has `name`, `description`, and `input_schema`. The name regex is `^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,64}$`. The four `tool_choice` types on the define-tools page are auto, any, tool, and none. `any` forces one of the provided tools without naming it. `tool` forces a named tool. Not every model supports forced tool use; where it does not, auto and none still work and the forced forms fail. Strict tool use, `strict: true`, is how they say you get schema-valid inputs when combined with a forced choice on models that support it. [cite:4]
MCP, as the 2025-11-25 spec defines it

The specification says MCP is an open protocol for connecting LLM applications to external data and tools, inspired by the Language Server Protocol’s idea of one standard for many clients. Messages are JSON-RPC 2.0. A host is the LLM application that initiates connections. A client is the connector inside the host. A server is the service that offers capabilities. The authoritative schema is the TypeScript schema the spec points at; this room cites the written specification, not a blog recap. [cite:5]

rows: Functions for the AI model to execute — meaning the model selects them; your host still runs client-side effects. [cite:5]
Model-selected, host-executed. Discovery is `tools/list`. Invocation is `tools/call`. A tool has a name and an input schema. [cite:7]
Context and data for the user or the model. [cite:5]
Application-selected reads. Do not treat a resource fetch as a side effect. If it is a side effect, it was a tool.
Templated messages and workflows for users. [cite:5]
User-invoked templates. They are not hidden system prompts the model discovers alone.
Server-initiated agentic behaviors and recursive LLM calls. [cite:5]
The server asks the host to run a model. The spec says users must explicitly approve sampling, and that the protocol limits what the server sees of the prompt. [cite:5]
Server-initiated questions about which URIs or filesystem boundaries it may use. [cite:5]
A boundary, not a blank check on the disk.
Server-initiated requests for more information from the user. [cite:5]
A question back to the human. It is not a reason to scrape their files.

blocks.text: The tools page says servers that support tools must declare the tools capability. Clients discover tools with `tools/list`, which supports pagination. They invoke with `tools/call`. The input schema is JSON Schema. The spec revision we read requires JSON Schema 2020-12 support for schemas that do not name a dialect. [cite:5] [cite:7] If a tutorial shows a different method name, the tutorial is behind the spec or ahead of it. Check the revision date. This room is pinned to 2025-11-25.

Transports in that revision: stdio, and Streamable HTTP. Clients should support stdio whenever possible. The server process on stdio is launched by the client; the spec’s transport page is the authority for framing, and this room does not paraphrase byte-level rules it has not quoted in full. Streamable HTTP uses a single endpoint that supports POST and GET. The client sends JSON-RPC as HTTP POST and must accept either a JSON body or a server-sent event stream. GET can open a stream for server-initiated messages. This transport replaces HTTP+SSE from protocol version 2024-11-05. On HTTP, the client must send `MCP-Protocol-Version` on subsequent requests, for example `2025-11-25`. A missing header is specified to fall back to assuming `2025-03-26` when the server has no other way to know. An unsupported version is a 400. [cite:6]

Security, from the spec’s own principles: users must consent to and understand data access and operations; hosts must not transmit resource data elsewhere without consent; tools are arbitrary code execution; descriptions and annotations are untrusted unless the server is trusted; hosts must obtain explicit consent before invoking a tool; sampling requires explicit approval, including what the server is allowed to see back. The spec says the protocol itself cannot enforce these, and that implementors should build the consent UI. [cite:5] A contact-center host that auto-approves `refund` because the description said “safe” has ignored that paragraph.
How the pieces sit together

You can ship an agent with no MCP: one host, one provider’s tool schema, your functions. You can ship MCP with no “agent” brand: a host that lists tools and calls one because the user clicked it, which is closer to a prompt or a resource than to a free-running loop. The combination people mean in 2026 is a host loop whose available tools are the union of MCP servers the user connected. OpenAI’s built-in MCP tool is one host’s way of doing that inside their API. It does not remove the spec, and it does not mean every MCP server is safe to attach to a voice bot. [cite:2] [cite:5]

Retrieval from T3 becomes a tool whose arguments are the question and the audience filter, and whose result is packed chunks. The model must not be the component that drops the filter. The host passes the filter in, or the tool reads it from a server-side session that the model cannot edit. That is the bridge from T3 to this room.

One tool call through MCP. Steps match the table. Approval is a host step, not a model step.
Diagram: Sequence of initialize, tools list, model tool call, approval, tools call, result, final answer

Scenario: a caller on a voice bot says “move me to billing.” The host has an MCP server that exposes `transfer_to_queue`. The queue name is an argument. The side effect is real. The walk-through refuses to skip consent.

rows: Capability negotiation. Pin the protocol revision you tested. This room uses 2025-11-25. [cite:5]
Names, descriptions, input schemas. Treat descriptions as untrusted if you did not author the server. [cite:5] [cite:7]
The transcript can be wrong. T7 owns recognition. Log the text you actually sent.
Provider JSON, not MCP frames. OpenAI’s five-step flow or Anthropic’s tool_use round trip. [cite:2] [cite:3]
If you forced `tool` or `any` on Anthropic, do not expect a preamble. [cite:4]
Spec: explicit consent before invoke. A voice bot speaks the confirmation and waits. [cite:5]

Only after allow. Include an idempotency key your server understands. The spec requires the call shape; the key is your addition. The changelog since 2025-06-18, fetched 2026-10-14, does not add an idempotency field. [cite:12]
Reject unknown queue names. Do not let the model invent a destination outside the dial plan. This room does not publish dial-plan values.

Tool result bound to the call id
OpenAI: call id. Anthropic: `tool_use_id`. Do not mix the field names. [cite:2] [cite:3]
A short confirmation, or another call if the budget allows
Stop if the transfer already succeeded. A second call is how you transfer twice.

blocks.text: 05Config path

There is no single admin console for “agents.” You configure three places: the model provider (tool schema and tool_choice), the MCP host (which servers are connected, and the consent UI), and the server (which tools exist). The contact-center route that reaches this host still lives in Webex, UCCE, or CUCM. This room does not reproduce those menus.

items: Write the tool schema with a name, a description that says when not to call it, and a JSON schema for arguments. On Anthropic, check the name regex before the first request. [cite:4]
Choose `tool_choice` on purpose. Leave it on auto unless you have a reason to force a call. If you force it, update your parser for the missing preamble on Anthropic. [cite:4]
Register the MCP server on the host. Prefer stdio for a local process. For HTTP, set the endpoint and send `MCP-Protocol-Version`. [cite:6]
Declare the tools capability on the server and implement `tools/list` and `tools/call`. [cite:7]
Put side-effect tools behind a host approval step. Read the spec’s consent principle and implement a UI or a spoken confirm. Do not encode “always allow” because a demo was annoying. [cite:5]
Add a step budget and a token budget in the host. Log both when you stop.
Make the tool idempotent. Pass a key the server stores. A duplicate `tools/call` returns the original result.

Log model id, tool name, arguments with secrets redacted, allow/deny, result status, and protocol revision. Do not log raw payment data. GDPR Article 5(1)(e) is storage limitation, and OpenAI’s fetched API abuse-monitoring default is up to 30 days. This room does not invent the local archive’s integer. [cite:14] [cite:15]

blocks.title: Description is data
blocks.text: A server you did not write can put instructions in a tool description. The spec tells you to treat that text as untrusted. Show it to the user in the consent step or pin servers to an allow-list you review. [cite:5]
06Limits, licensing, gotchas
